en: *Abhayapaddhati*, Chapter 9: *Caryāpaṭala* (The Chapter on Conduct), Verse 1. Even though one has gained access to both stages (*ubhayakrama*), the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā does not occur without conduct (*caryā*). Therefore, he speaks of the *Caryāpaṭala*, beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.

Conduct (*caryā*) is the distinguished activity of body, speech, and mind. Because it transcends the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, and because it is superior to other forms of conduct, it is "supremely excellent" (*atyantavarā*).
She has gone by way of transcending the world.
In some places, the reading is "an exceedingly beautiful woman" (*atyantavarāṅganām*); in that case, the words "having taken her" (*tām ādāya*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And this [practice] should not be performed impulsively out of restlessness; thus he says, "The eight siddhis," and so forth.

These are the siddhis of the underworld, collyrium, foot-ointment, the pill, invisibility, the sword, mercury, and the elixir, or alternatively, the eight qualities of sovereign power (*aṣṭaiśvarya*).
For one who has attained this capacity, when there is a desire [to practice], the conduct is authorized;
because such a person, being devoted to yoga, becomes heedful,
and adversaries do not overcome him.
Indeed, he becomes capable of both restraining and favoring them,
and is not overcome by cold, heat, and so forth;
because he is unassailed by the eight worldly concerns and other such factors, he is completely liberated from all obscurations.
Because he has attained equality with space,
having a single flavor identical to the sameness of all phenomena;
this is the state of emptiness.
At the time of requesting alms, when donors have made a refusal by saying "no," one should practice the meditation on the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena.
"Meditation" here refers to the cultivation of skillful means;
it is the unsurpassed non-duality of wisdom and skillful means.
Devoted to the Dharma, he is continuously engaged in that non-dual reality.
Regarding the passage beginning with "dravya" and so forth:

through contentment with whatever food happens to be available, and by means of the continuous flow of yoga—attained through specific practice according to one's preference in particular places, times, and conditions—the thick darkness of the cave accumulated over a long time [is dispelled] like the flame of a lamp.
The collective meaning is that one should realize Mahāmudrā by removing even a vast accumulation of the defects of conceptual construction, though gathered over a long period of time.
The phrase "of one engaged in the yoga of conduct" (*caryāyogayuktasya*) uses the genitive case in the sense of the locative.
It refers to the *Buddhakapāla-tantra*, a tantra of twelve thousand verses.
(2) "10. It is pure by its own nature. If the world were pure by its very essence (*svarūpeṇa*), then everyone would effortlessly attain Mahāmudrā; what need would there be for the practice of yoga?
But was it not said: "Conceptual construction (*viyappa*) must be destroyed"?
Therefore it has been said by Jñānapāda: "There is indeed no other suffering of existence than the activity of natural conceptualization;
and this [state] is directly perceived by the mind as its opposite."
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Abhayapaddhati.
(3) Chapter 1: The Ritual for Bathing with Ten Divine Great Medicinal Herbs. To explain the means for one who is intent upon benefiting others, he says "atha" and so forth.
"Sattvārthaikasuniścayam" refers to that in which the singular purpose of sentient beings is perfectly determined.
"Hemaka" is so called because it shines or makes manifest like gold (*hema*).
Of coral, [the word] *pravāla* [is used].
By "by which" is meant by gold.
"Possessing wealth through pearls and other riches" means they become wealthy.
He indicates the general statement that those [substances] are not external herbs mentioned in other tantras, using the words "nor even" and so forth.
"Of another metal" means another metal;
however, the efficacious herb is internal.
3. *Rajasya*, [the genitive of] *rajas*.

4. *Ke te*, *kā sā*—(4) 5. "Accomplished through recitation" (*paṭhitasiddhā*) means she whose mantra is accomplished (*siddha*) by means of internal muttering (*antarjalpa*) once it has been recited (*paṭhita*).
6. That and this are accomplished:
in the vessel, the divine medicine within the lotus of wisdom.
7. "Essence" refers to the *bodhicitta*.
In the center of the lotus,
she who leads the *rasa* (vital essence) from the upper station downward is the *rasanī*, that is, the *avadhūtī*;
he resides within her.
"By youth" means a young woman of sixteen years. "And he" means she and the Tathāgata, [referring to] the yogin of the *Buddhakapāla*.
He is pitiless,
and they are pitiless;
however, the absence of pity arises from the conjunction with *rajas*.

9. It is not accomplished; the meaning is that the simultaneous emission of the seminal fluids of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) is the basis for accomplishment (*siddhi*). 10. [The phrase] "of the Buddhas" is to be connected with the term "the state of the Leader.
Even by means of simultaneous emission while maintaining [the state] for only a few moments, the great medicine accomplishes gold.
The intended meaning is that when it is maintained without limit, it becomes Buddhahood consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
A steadfast person should impel it; then that great medicinal herb must perform its function.
The moon, the semen;
smeared, even with blood.
Therein, in the moon.
Meru, the sound "suṃ.
(5) 12. [One should] place the effect, the meditative attainment, [within it].
One should perform the ritual deposit (nikṣepa).
The object is the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Left and right.
The two channels.
"Contracted" is an adverbial modifier.
And contraction is said to be the means for preventing rapid emission.
However, it must be clearly understood through instruction.

For instance, by contracting the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds according to the instruction, and through the stability of the mind, the fluctuations of the mind are brought under control; consequently, there gradually arise the non-falling from its own place, the non-emission externally, and the increase of the *bodhicitta*.

That indeed is the aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa) here; however, one whose passion is for gold and such things leaks [the essence], and for this very reason he says: "Together," meaning that wisdom and means should be applied simultaneously.
Some say that "tāmrapala" refers to the substance;
it is located at the noose, on the left side of Prajñā.
Some point out that it is within another lotus.
"13. Subsequently, 'action' refers to meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
In the phrase beginning with 'of Sumeru,' the genitive case is used in the sense of the first [case]."
The seed-syllable king is the syllable *hrīḥ*.
14. Molasses, a copper ball, the wise one, and the practitioner of deity yoga.
One should perform the protection with the heart-mantras and so forth.

This is the meaning: having oneself become the form of the Bhagavān, embraced by a young woman in the form of the Bhagavatī, one should contemplate within one’s own heart the *bodhicitta* in the shape of a moon disc, mixed with all the elixir of accomplishment (*siddharasa*) and blood; above that, the seed-syllable *suṃ*; and above that, the syllable *hrīḥ*. These three, having melted together with the *bodhicitta* produced from the union of passion (*mahārāga*), flow down and fall into the lotus along with the pollen of the wisdom consort’s *bodhicitta*.
Having quickly smeared copper or iron with that heated mixture, one should cast it into the fire.
Furthermore, the Buddha is not unauthoritative;
therefore, "this" and so forth [is established].
"Whatever object" refers to that which has been stated and that which is yet to be stated;
it is immeasurable, a superimposition of the immeasurable.
They do not decline; they are not abandoned from hell.
17. "Four," and so forth:
this unsurpassed *Yoginītantra* is the secret essence of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*).
18. Regarding "gold and silver as well": copper becomes gold and iron becomes silver;
one should take this very [iron], heated, along with one *raktikā* of pure mercury, and administer it as a nasal drop (*nasya*) every day for six months.
Its benefit is that one lives, and so forth;
[it occurs] in the union of the vajra and the lotus.
20. "Four" is stated because the victory flask (vijayakalaśa) is established as primary even though it was not explicitly mentioned.

21. Here, regarding the consecration of the vase (*kalaśādhivāsana*) as described in the fourth chapter, he states the specific detail: "of oneself" means with the blood of one's own name, mixed with the primary element (*pradhānadhātu*) of a barren woman.
22. "Black, red, and most terrible" means that which is most terrible by virtue of both the color black and the color red.
The meaning here is that the Lord is black, embraced by the red vital essence (*citrasena*), and surrounded here by the retinue of the eight goddesses.
Some teachers, however, say that one who is black and slightly red is indeed devoid of wisdom.

This is the meaning: here, the master—being the very self of Heruka together with his retinue—having offered the bali-offerings to the ten directions at the eastern gate of a mandala or cloth-mandala that has been prepared according to the ritual rules and worshipped with the fivefold offerings;

Having consecrated five vases whose interiors are smeared with the primary red element and whose mouths are turned downward, one should bathe a barren woman who is facing the mandala immediately after the menstrual flow, at the time of her ritual bath following menstruation.
Rising oneself, one should first bathe her while reciting the heart mantra and the syllable *HŪṂ* with a display of majesty using the *Vijaya* vase.
At that very moment, immeasurable heroes and heroines, drawn by the rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, bathe her with vases filled with bodhicitta held in their sprout-like hands.

At that very moment, four fierce men— incarnations of the single-svabhāva Heruka, devoid of [ordinary] intellect and wielding swords— simultaneously strike the sky with their swords with the intent to slay the Māras such as the Grahas;
in this manner, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the other vases in sequence,
and thereafter, one should gratify him.
Thereupon she shall become pregnant with a son; likewise, one whose sons have died shall come to have living sons. This is the tenth chapter from the *Abhayapaddhati*.
(8) Chapter 11: The Definitive Instruction on the Practice of the Vidyādharas. He speaks, beginning with "Now," in order to explain the practice of the Vidyādharas.
All that was previously stated regarding the procedure for the *śālikā* practice in the fourth chapter is to be understood here as well.
He states the specific distinction: "by this very [method]," referring to what is about to be described.

3. Regarding the passage beginning with "kāladaṣṭaka," etc.: when one has been bitten by Kāla (Death) and is abandoned by all the Gāruḍikas because they are powerless [to cure him], thinking he is "bitten by Kāla," then one should undertake the ritual action.
"Śukladehā" means that the Blessed One and the goddesses of the cardinal directions are white,
while the goddesses of the intermediate directions are red;
"according to rule" means by means of the accomplishment of the three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
5. A sword made of ground śāli rice;
6. Of those two vidyādharas;
one should draw and cast it.
On a leaf such as birch-bark;
(7) with the sprout of white karavīra;
(9) "in one" means a single vidyādhara.
It falls upon the bitten person;
at that very moment, the bitten person rises up.
Thus, the methods for making one like rice, for making one like water, and for making one a Vidyādhara have been described.
The other fifteen instruments are to be known as they are taught in the *Buddhakapālatantra* in twelve thousand [verses].
This is the eleventh chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*.
(10) Chapter 12: The Application of Various Mantras. Regarding the instruction on the accomplishment of *añjana* (collyrium), he says "atha" and so forth.
[It refers to] the preeminent among the twenty-four yoginīs. "Seen, seen" means those who have been beheld.
"In which" means in those [tantras].
"Not spoken" means not taught in other tantras.
"Highly fortunate" means praiseworthy, because they are the recipients of great qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) that are free from obscurations.
Because she is intent upon the welfare of sentient beings, she is said to be the perfection of the benefit of others;
because her nature consists of the state of the cause, she is the mother of all Buddhas;
and because she is the nature of the fruit, she is Mahāmudrā.
The yogis [are] of the yogis;
all have attained a wonder by all— meaning,
having attained certainty regarding the power of laughter— is the ellipsis.
A person is like a banner;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is triangular. In that very same pit...
With the head [he strikes] upon the head, that is, upon the skull;
of that flesh;
8. another [he strikes] upon another skull.
(11) 9 "Of the obstacle" means obstacles;
"lampblack" means completely.
10 "One should drink" means oneself.
11. "One should cause [her] to drink" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).

12. Here, the yogin of Buddhakapāla, in a cremation ground, having prepared a triangular hearth from the hip-bone of a suspended human corpse, and having placed upon it a wick made of a shroud from the cremation ground soaked in the oil of the flesh from that same hip—within a skull-cup filled with that oil—and having lit it with a cremation-ground fire, he should, while reciting the mantra, cause soot to fall from another suspended human skull placed above it.

Taking that *kañjala* (semen) which has not touched the ground with both hands first, and then placing it in the left hand, one should slowly desire a maiden who wears a garland of yellow flowers, whose virginity is intact, who possesses a flow of *rajas*, and who is visualized as Citrasenā; having tasted a small portion of the *bodhicitta* mixed with *rajas* with both hands, one should rub it together with the remainder using the right ring finger and thumb.

Then, having made one hundred and eight pills from her very menstrual blood, and having consecrated each pill one hundred and eight times while reciting the mantra, one should anoint the eyes with it; such is the collective meaning.
(13) The phrase "by this very [mantra]" is connected with "having anointed" and so forth.
O Mahābāhu Vajrapāṇi, because your arms are intent upon satisfying all sentient beings.
The supreme Yoginī is most easily attained here in the Yoginītantra. (12) 14 "With the ring finger and the thumb" refers to the right hand.
Thus, in the subsequent case of applying collyrium, the activity belongs to the right hand.
15. "Bhadra" means he would be like one whose eyes have not been anointed due to the rubbing of the eyes.
16. He is seven *tāla* trees in height for the purpose of warding off excessive rain.
17. Regarding "of the Great-Souled One," the word "by his power" (*prabhāvāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
18. The genitive case in *svarūpaparivartanasya* is used in the sense of the first case (nominative).

19. Regarding *prayoga*: the applications for the accomplishment of states such as that of a Vidyādhara are not mentioned in the *Laghutantra*, but they are explained in detail; they should be learned from the mouth of the Guru. 20. To state the specific rosary (*akṣasūtra*) for each specific mantra recitation (*mantrajāpa*), he says: "Now," and so forth.
21. One should recite over an elephant bone for the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
22. A "great bone" (*mahāsthi*) refers to a human bone. 23. A "bird bone" (*śakunāsthi*) refers to a vulture bone.

24. With copper, with a copper thread. 25. All this elaborate detail has been taught even within the context of the generation stage (utpattikrama) in various ways out of consideration for those to be trained; but as for the completion stage (utpannakrama), what is the use of this? To this he says: "In the mind alone," and so forth.
Mind alone is the stainless mirror of the triple world;
for whatever is conceived by it appears like a reflection,
and all this is superimposed upon the mind.
And that mind, from the perspective of ultimate reality, is of the nature of a dream and devoid of all conceptual proliferation;
let those fools who do not know this remain possessed of the full power of their undiminished conceptual constructions.

Furthermore, even those who know [the truth] through hearing and so forth are nevertheless grasped by such conceptual constructions; thus, he has been moved by compassion with the intent to incite them toward the cultivation of the nature of reality, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
This is the twelfth chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*.

(14) Chapter 13: Purification of the Mind. It is said, beginning with "Now," etc., that in both stages (*krama*), reality itself (*tattva*) is the purification of all obscurations and stains; thus, it is called the "Chapter on Purification. Here, "purification" refers to the purified reality, and not merely reality alone.
Because reality (*tattva*) exists everywhere and at all times, it would follow that everyone would always be pure.

Furthermore, since that [reality] is not easy to realize without the reality of the means (*upāyatattva*), he says "sister" and so forth in order to show how it is to be realized by being endowed with those means through reliance upon the Vajrayāna;
this is according to the literal meaning for one of superior capacity.
Alternatively, the sister is one who has ascended the Vajrayāna;
her daughter is the niece;
and the mother is the bestower of initiation.
The daughter is affectionate, or she stands in her place;
5. "wise" because of pure knowledge;
6. "the Mahāmudrā" means to realize it directly.
By this, the reality of the object of attainment has been stated.
(15) 7. Ḍombinī is fond of meditation;
Nartakī is of skillful movement.
The washerwoman is devoted to pure virtues;
the outcaste woman (caṇḍālinī) is of a patient disposition because she has destroyed pride;
the leather-worker is devoted to the auspicious formative activities of the body of the three vajras.
Internally, however, wisdom (prajñā) is the sister, Lalanā;
the niece is Rasanā;
and the mother is Avadhūtī.
Through the teacher’s instruction, the union of the two preceding [channels] with the subsequent one is the daughter;
the great bliss arising from the union of those very three channels—which possess the nature of non-duality of wisdom and means—is the wife.
As it has been said: "That bliss is known as the beloved."
The consciousness of sound is Ḍombinī; the consciousness of taste is Nartakī;
the consciousness of touch is Dhovvinī.
Olfactory consciousness is Caṇḍālinī; visual consciousness is Carmakāriṇī.
As for the definitive meaning, the unsurpassed wisdom consisting of the sisters and so forth has been explained in the first chapter.
She is called *bhāryā* because she is filled by the two accumulations of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-saṃbhāra*).
She is a *ḍombinī* because, due to having the single flavor of emptiness (*śūnyatā-ekarasa*), she cannot be touched by any adventitious conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
She is "fickle" because she does not abide anywhere, owing to her non-abiding in either cyclic existence (*bhava*) or nirvāṇa.
She is a dancer (*nartakī*) because she performs a dance for those to be trained through the manifestation of various illusory forms. She is a flute-player (*dhovviṇī*) because,

by means of the gradual attainment of the softest [levels of concentration] and so forth, she washes away the stains of the obscurations along with their latent tendencies, starting from the highest of the high levels.
*Caṇḍā* is wisdom (*prajñā*) which ascertains the nature of that which has arisen;
*ālī* is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
She is called *Caṇḍālinī* because she leads these two to the unsurpassed state.

Because it tears apart the skin of ignorance that follows the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśabhavāṅga*), it is called "the leather-worker" (*carmakāriṇī*); thus, it is unsurpassed wisdom (*niruttarā prajñā*).
One should understand that these external and internal forms of wisdom possess the status of "wisdom" because they imitate these very qualities of unsurpassed wisdom.
For this very reason, he will say: "by means of purifying the impure mind."
12. By this, in the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*), external wisdom (*prajñā*) is the action-seal (*karmamudrā*);
internal wisdom is the dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*);
and unsurpassed wisdom is the great seal (*mahāmudrā*).
Because it is established upon this very foundation of purity;
the Dharma-seal is the Dharmakāya,
because its intrinsic nature is the mind of great bliss.
The body adorned with the primary and secondary marks, encapsulated by the *karmamudrā*, is the *saṃbhogakāya*. The *samayamudrā*—

which manifests in the form of infinite, diverse, and boundless maṇḍala wheels and so forth— is the *nirmāṇakāya*, because it does not fail to appear at the opportune moment for the benefit of those disciples who are ready to be trained.
Mahāmudrā, however, is all-pervasive; it is the fourth body, the svābhāvikakāya.
Alternatively, Mahāmudrā is the sambhogakāya, possessing a form endowed with the major marks, minor signs, radiant arms, faces, and emblems.
Samayamudrā is the nature of the mind, personally realized within; it is the dharmakāya.
For it is said that "the occasion" (*samaya*) is indeed awakening.

The Dharma-mudrā, being the empowerment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), consists of various forms and has speech as its nature that reveals the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*).
The Karma-mudrā, because its form is the performance of activities, accomplishes tasks through various emanations and is thus the Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

In the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), the external wisdom (*bāhyaprajñā*) herself, who has been meditated upon in the form of the chosen goddess, is the action seal (*karmamudrā*); she is also known by the alternative name "the consort of one's own nature" (*svābhāṅganā*).
Furthermore, that which is meditated upon within the body as the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth is the dharma seal (*dharmamudrā*).

The *samayamudrā* refers to the deities who have merged within the maṇḍala circle produced from the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and so forth, performing the emanation and reabsorption [of light] and so on; it also refers to the hand-symbol (*cihna*).
It is indicated that the *mahāmudrā* is the very form of the presiding deity (*nāyakadevatā*) oneself.
To explain that internal wisdom (*prajñā*) itself takes the form of the sense faculties, the afflictions, and the objects of the senses, he says: "Now," and so forth.
16. "Taste" refers to the tongue.
17. "Mind" refers here to the body-faculty as characterized by the mind.

18. From the words to be spoken later, such as "How could form be a sister?", it should be understood that the objects of form and so forth—such as form being a sister and so on—are indicated by way of illustration for the eye and the other faculties.
19. "As for 'this': that which is form (*rūpa*) is delusion (*moha*) because it is a cause of delusion.
Due to the connection with the word 'also' (*api*), there is also hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth;
and as for passion (*rāga*), there is also [attachment] to passion."
Pride is indeed pride;
envy as well.
Because objects such as form and so forth give rise to delusion and the like, they are designated as "delusion" and so on.
But not in reality—this is the meaning.
20 "Of the mind" means that these particular states of the mind itself, such as the eye, delusion, form, and so forth, are merely states of the mind;
and the mind is indeed impure due to the stains of delusion and the like.
Therefore, the intention is that the eyes and so forth are also impure. [Objection:
How then is it said that these are the wisdoms (prajñā) such as the "Sister" and so on? [Reply: He says, "Therefore," because these are indeed pure wisdoms.
The purity of their minds alone is their purity;
therefore, one should purify the mind.
To the question "Who [should do this]?", he says: "the one of great wisdom."
Great wisdom is Mahāmudrā; one who cultivates that [wisdom] is so called because by that very [wisdom] all stains are washed away.

For this very reason, it says "of the mind of ultimate yoga," meaning one whose single flavor is the non-duality of wisdom and means, having transcended the extremes of existence, non-existence, and so forth.

23. If one does not meditate in this way, then accomplishment—the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā—will not occur. However, when through diligent and uninterrupted meditation there arises purity consisting of great bliss known by oneself, that is accomplishment in this very human birth. One who desires accomplishment should not remain for even a moment with a mind directed elsewhere.

(19) Thus, according to the word of the Blessed One, when the accumulations of merit and wisdom consisting of uninterrupted cultivation are fulfilled with diligence in a single [life], [one attains purity]. However, in the absence of such cultivation, one obtains in another existence—after an indefinite number of births—a life free from the eight inopportune states (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*) and conducive to practice; through that practice, one becomes purified. In the system of the *pāramitās*, however, it is stated that purification occurs over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) due to the accumulation of merit consisting of ritual action and the absence of specific skillful means (*upāya*); thus, there is no contradiction.

26. But surely, nothing here is taught as something to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), since only mudrās that have already arisen in form are indicated, and because it is through them alone that yogins are thus pointed out.
True.
Since, in reality, the object of meditation, the meditator, and the act of meditation are untenable because all phenomena are primordially quiescent,
he demonstrates this with the words "non-existence," and so forth.
In non-existence— that is, in the negation of the superimposition of existence and in non-arising, which is the ultimate truth— how could there be any entity or any act of meditation?
Because of its primordial purity.
28. Now, if non-arising is reality, one might ask: "Does that which is to be cultivated exist? To this he says: "Of what nature is non-existence?"
There is no non-arising;
however, because it is conducive to the realization of the ultimate, the ultimate is called "reality.
Furthermore, even that entity which consists of conventional truth is not to be conceived as a non-entity, because it is a truth.

(20) The meaning is that for those who have attained the stage of the simultaneous union (*yuganaddha-krama*), there is no longer any dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*) to the notions of "that which is to be realized," "the realizer," or "the process of realization," since liberation arises merely from seeing the non-duality of the two truths.
As it is said in the *Śrī-samāja*: "In the absence [of entities], there is no cultivation; cultivation itself is not cultivation.
Thus, being is not being, and cultivation is not perceived."
Thus [it is said].
30 For this very reason, he concludes: "How could it be? refers to the cultivation [of the thought];
therefore, the meaning is that it is not perceived.
31. Is it then that in the stage of the arisen (utpannakrama) there is merely the cessation of cultivation? It is not cessation. 32. Then, what is it like?
The nature of that [emptiness] will be explained.
(33) Having thus refuted attachment to the "cultivator" and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality, and desiring to refute attachment to form and so forth, he says: "Sister," and so on.
(34) How so? Because form is divided by distinctions such as "fair-skinned" and so forth.
It is "conjoined" with the sense faculty because they are connected through a state of mutual assistance;
one with an impure mind will see it, but not one with a pure mind.
From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), this is because the sense faculties, their objects, and the cognitions thereof lack intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*).
The same applies hereafter.
(21) 35 "Threefold" refers to the distinction between the agreeable, the disagreeable, and the neutral.
36. "Of one endowed with such yoga" means one who is engaged in the yoga of Mahāmudrā. 37. "That which is smelled" refers to the nose, [and by extension] to odor.
38. "Unseen" means not being perceived or not being known.
For this very reason, passion, aversion, and so forth do not arise from odors and the like.
Regarding the phrase "of that which has the nature of taste," it means that the essential nature of taste does not exist,
because of the absence of both the tongue and flavor.
By means of the body-faculty characterized by the mind,
one experiences pleasure born from the object of touch; by implication, one also experiences pain and equanimity.
And what is that like?
The mental faculty (*manas*), being mental, experiences pleasure— and by way of illustration, pain, joy, dejection, and equanimity.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "What, moreover, is that like?

However, the consciousness that has just passed away is called the mental faculty (*manas*) because it exercises sovereignty over the arising of the subsequent six specific consciousnesses;
its specific features are the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which takes them as its object.

The two [types of] conceptualization, however, have the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

these same [elements], when condensed, are the twelve bases (āyatanas),
and in extreme brevity, they are the five aggregates (skandhas).
And those very [beings] belong to the three realms, and that is mind-only.

Thus [it is said].
And that mind is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
As it is stated in that very same place: "The teaching of the Sage that 'all this is mind-only'..."
It is for the purpose of removing the fear of the ignorant; it does not exist in reality.

50. If it is then asked whether the investigating mind exists as ultimate reality, he says: "Investigation" (*vicāram*); since it investigates, it is called "investigation. Thus, the consciousness that is the investigator does not exist there when both are being investigated.

As it was said by the venerable teacher Śāntideva: "When that which is to be investigated has been investigated, there is no further basis for investigation. Because it lacks a basis, it does not arise; and that is called nirvāṇa."
51. Likewise: When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind, then, due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes supportless and is stilled.
Thus it is said.
And in the *Rājaratnāvalī*, it is stated: "All the phenomena of the world are considered to be the fuel for the fire of primordial wisdom;
having burned them with the flames of correct analytical discernment, one attains peace. (25)
Thus [it is asked]: "How is there an investigation of both?
To this he says: "Existence," and so forth.
There is no identity between existence and non-existence because they are contradictory.
To show that there is a distinction, he says: "Existence and non-existence are both empty.
This means that the intrinsic natures of existence and non-existence are empty.
Because the mind is devoid of a nature that is either unitary or manifold, it is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
For instance, it is not a unity;
if it were a unity, there would be no cognition appearing as variegated through the forms of blue and yellow.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that everything—yellow and so forth—would be perceived as being included within the blue.
Furthermore, there would be no perception of the blue itself as having distinctions of front, back, and middle, nor as appearing as something gross.
For that which possesses a distinction of spatial parts cannot logically be a single unity.
(26) According to this reasoning, the appearance would have to consist of nothing more than a single atom.
Nor can it be manifold;

for if the mind were manifold, it would be divided into atoms, and since there is no cognition of anything other than that [mind], each atom would exist as a form of self-cognition. Consequently, the undesirable consequence follows that there would be an appearance corresponding to each individual atom.
57. Even a dual nature is not tenable, because there is no such experience. For in all cases, our perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And we do not perceive any direct perceptual awareness (*saṃvitti*) that possesses both a positive and a negative form, whether simultaneously or separately.
Or [it might be] of the nature of inference, because that [inference] is preceded by that [perception].
And not perceiving [any such basis], how could we imagine that which lacks a means of valid cognition to have the nature of both inclusion and exclusion?

59. Now, consciousness in the form of its own self-awareness, appearing as a variegated gross form, exists as something that cannot be denied; and since that [consciousness] could not exist without having the nature of both the inclusive (anugata) and the exclusive (vyāvṛtta), it is postulated through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti) based on the existence of those [two forms]. 60. That is not so.
Because it is more clearly established as being free from conceptual proliferation precisely by way of being neither of these two forms, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted.
For this very reason, even arising is not tenable,
since there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the relationship between cause and effect.
For the determination of the causal relationship between cause and effect occurs when means of valid cognition function in a sequence of priority and posteriority;
and a non-dual consciousness that is devoid of two forms does not possess such sequential operation.
It has been established that there is no further cognition [of that], due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And since, in this way, because of the absence of any means of valid cognition for the relation of cause and effect, there is no arising at all, then how could it arise from itself, from another, from both, or without a cause?
Thus, because there is no arising, the mind does not even exist as a positive entity.
For that which "comes to be" is established as an existence (*bhāva*) consisting solely in manifestation preceded by non-existence (*asattā*).
For this very reason, it does not possess the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) characterized by the falling away from that [existence].

And because there is an absence of the intrinsic nature of both existence and non-existence, there is the absence of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), since all such proliferation is pervaded by those two, insofar as they serve as the substratum for existence and non-existence.
And because the pervaded is absent when the pervader is absent,
through this investigation, the state of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*)— emptiness— is understood.
And this alone is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).
That which is the non-perception of all phenomena when one investigates with the eye of wisdom, once the light of right knowledge has arisen.
As it is said in the *Bhagavatī*: "What is the wisdom-eye of the Blessed Buddhas?
It is that by which they do not see anything."
Likewise, what is the vision of ultimate reality?
It is the non-seeing of all phenomena.
(28) Thus it is said.
65. Therefore, even those who practice the yoga of reality, though established in all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) and perceiving all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), do not see them.
Such non-perception is what is intended here, and not that which arises from a lack of mental attention (*amanasikāra*), as in the case of one who is asleep or whose eyes are closed.

For if the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) are not thus abandoned, then—just as in the case of one who has emerged from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and so forth—the yogin would remain unliberated due to the re-emergence of passion and other afflictions rooted in the attachment to form and the like.

Furthermore, attachment to form and the like, which is beginningless, is not abandoned merely by the avoidance of mental attention (*manasikāra*), because that would entail the absurd consequence that even those who have entered the attainment of non-perception would have abandoned it.
Nor is it possible to avoid such mental attention without abandoning doubt regarding objects such as form.

Just as one avoids being burned by avoiding the fire, so too, because the seed of doubt has been removed, it is certain that attachment to form and so forth must be eliminated— not by pulling it out like a thorn, but by its very disappearance. Thus,
by setting aside mental engagement with existence, non-existence, intrinsic nature, extrinsic nature, and so on, and withdrawing the mind from everything, one should not think of anything at all.

As he was reflecting in this way, there arose for that very yogi—who had long served his guru even before—his venerable Prajñā, attained through the grace of the guru. By means of the yoga of non-perception (*adarśana-yoga*), he directly realized her nature as supreme bliss, because she is free from the distinctions between the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results; because her own nature is self-luminous and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); and because she is the cessation of the flood of suffering that is the very nature of saṃsāra, which consists of conceptual proliferation.

"By its power—alas, how great is the capacity of delusion!—these beings do not realize that their very self is of the nature of *nirvāṇa*. How indeed might I cause them to realize this? Then, having arisen in the form of the maṇḍala of that very nature, one’s own self—the nature of all phenomena—is [unified] with the Blessed Lady Prajñā, who is of the nature of great compassion and is otherwise named Mahāmudrā, because of being of that same nature.
One should perceive them as having an undifferentiated nature;

No; for action is of two kinds, distinguished as that which is originated and that which originates. Among these, all bodily and vocal action is that which is originated, whereas mental action is that which originates.
And that is of two kinds:
consisting of non-greed and so forth, and its opposite.
Among these, all unwholesome actions of body and speech are originated from greed and so forth.

However, everything arising from non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth is indeed wholesome.

Therefore, the cultivation of the non-dual *bodhicitta*, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*), alone purifies all misdeeds and brings about all that is auspicious. As it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna: "This Mahāyāna is supreme; this *bodhicitta* is the highest.
With focused minds, let them generate *bodhicitta* with diligent effort."

That which consists of the four stages conducive to penetration, the ten stages,
and the state of fruition— all that has arisen from this yoga.

He will explain the abiding in silence as follows: "Salutation to that one who is non-dual, supreme bliss, and who is awake due to the absence of the sleep consisting of all remaining obscurations and latent tendencies.
By this verse, it is stated that this very wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), having arisen in a specific form like water in the form of waves, is the fourth consecration.
Furthermore, this Vajradhara, who consists of great bliss, is the source of all tantras.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapālamahātantra*, composed by the scholar Abhayākaragupta.
(45) Having severed the delusion of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through the lofty, rising, auspicious light of the exposition of the path of the glorious hero Heruka, may he dissolve into that very maṇḍala.
But I, as this world, shall for a long time bear the infinite forms of that Sage, bestowing abundant bliss upon every living being who bows before him, while destroying the phenomenal expansion.
The master Abhaya of Vikramaśīla composed this [work], which touches upon the vital points of speech, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of Rāmapāla. || 2 ||

(46) This work has been composed at the request of the illustrious Yakṣapāla, son of the Lord of Magadha, whose splendor brings about the fulfillment of steadfastness through his power; he is one who has conquered the three worlds, whose form is inexhaustible, and who is exalted by the non-dual Dharma for the benefit of the world. 3.

May the Goddess Prajñāśrī be victorious—she who is the ground of repose for the exuberant bliss of the non-dual supreme flavor arising from the root of bliss; she who is the playground for the assembly of sages crowded with Vajrakanyā; and she who is a wish-fulfilling creeper for seekers whose goals have been accomplished, serving as a flight of stairs to her. May there be satisfaction through the drinking of the peerless nectar of auspiciousness, using this commentary of ours as the provisions for the journey. || 4 ||
The total measure of this work, when condensed by scholars, consists of one hundred and sixteen verses; it truly resides in the hearts of the wise as its very essence. (47)
